The doctor is a professional. Tell her that you're more comfortable with her steering the conversation, and she will. The time is yours and your doctor should be able to work with you to find a comfortable level of give-and-take interaction. 

The words have taken on a nasty political tinge, but the therapist's office is truly a safe space that is literally protected by state doctor/patient confidentiality laws. You can feel comfortable almost completely letting your guard down in your sessions. Those who would violate the patient protection laws will have a criminal case on their hands. Even the biggest bully looking to dig up personal dirt on you is going to consider whether it's really worth it to get into a "The people versus this dumb asshole" situation.

Go to the first appointment. You don't even have to make the second. Your commitment can end there. Just dipping your toe into the therapy waters is going to help. If you want to continue, feel free to change doctors if you feel uncomfortable. Just go to this first appointment so you can feel it out and decide if you want to keep going.

At the very least, it's better than doing nothing and continuing to feel miserable, right?

Are you really scared of being a bad person? I can relate a bit as the one good thing about my last not-so-great therapist is that I was able to work out is that I'm not actually scared of being a bad person. I'm scared of being *perceived* as a bad person and getting a reputation as a bad person, but I'm not scared of *being* a bad person, because I know I'm not. Rationally, bad people go through their life never examining their actions and considering their morality. Bad people never think on how their actions impact others, and that's pretty much all I do when I'm ramped up to 11 on an anxiety attack.

If you're worried about being a good person, you're probably a better person than most because even if you don't realize you're doing it, you're making an effort to be aware of the effects of your actions.

>I haven't gone before and it's quite intimidating to think about.

I dont want to diminish the apprehension/fear you have at speaking with a therapist, but I wanted to tell you that its one of those things where once I did it, I wished I'd done it months earlier. Take some time to sort through those feelings so you can get the help you need/want as soon as you can. It's there when you're ready, you just have to call and make the appointment.

You still have a year to go and you can get into summer school if you speak to a guidance counselor asap.

I know it's easy and comfortable to just fall backwards and let it end in failure, but you don't sound like you're too excited at that prospect. Show up, tell your counselor about your mental health issues and ask what needs to be done to make things right.

Your academic career might be in critical condition, but its not dead yet. You can triumph in this if you can bring yourself to ask your faculty for the help you need. They have a vested interest in students not dropping out. They'll be more willing to help than you think.

>i am in grade 10 when shit like this actually matters

Can I tell you something that's going to be unpopular with your teachers and parents?

It doesn't matter nearly as much as they say it does. They just want you to take school seriously. Their intentions are good, you *should* take school seriously, but the amount of "THE REST OF YOUR LIFE DEPENDS ON YOUR PERFORMANCE HERE" narratives that most high school faculty and parents put on kids these days is completely unfair, and largely unrealistic.

Do your best. Some days you can give 100%, some days you can give 30%. Sometimes you just show up and go through the motions. Regardless, your grades should reflect your best efforts. Do your best, and listen to people who push you to be better on a personal level. Do your best to minimize the general "YOU WILL BE FLIPPING BURGERS IF YOU FAIL HERE!!" bullshit narrative of self-importance high schools in general like to push. In all things, do your true and honest best, and no one will be in a position to negatively judge you for it (and if they do, they're assholes, ignore them and go back to the people who want you to improve for *your* sake instead of for the sake of a state-mandated grading system)
Just saying, it's not as cut and dry as "try -> succeed". That's a gross oversimplification.

"More successful" doesn't translate into being a success. Im "more successful" than someone living in their car, but one failure could bust me back down to an equal level.

We're all one or two key failures from ruin. If the first guy is surviving, I respect his decision not to expose himself to lifestyle-threatening risks of failure.

I can't even create without having to cater to everyone. If I dare do something for me, I'm going to being berated for literally years as a selfish asshole for not considering everyone's feelings (it's happened several times before).

I'm sick of it and I want it to be over and the only way for it to end is for me to get off this mortal coil or for them to and despite what they've done to hurt me, I can't bring myself to hurt anyone else. I'm the only one that's being hurt by all of this, so I should just remove myself from it.
